newsitem.title: CHINA: China's Shanghai city income gap widening.
newsitem.headline: China's Shanghai city income gap widening.

text.p: The income gap in the booming eastern Chinese city of Shanghai is widening, with the richest 10 percent of residents now making nearly four times more than the poorest, the China Daily Business Weekly said on Sunday.
Shanghai residents in the top 10 percent income bracket made an average of 14,953 yuan ($1,800) in 1996 while those in the bottom 10 percent earned 3,785 yuan, the newspaper said.
That meant the income gap between the two groups was 11,168 yuan last year, compared with a difference of 1,964 yuan in 1990, the newspaper said.
"Although the city's population has not been polarised into rich and poor extremes, the income gap is widening," it said.
The highest salary earners in the city of 13 million people were entrepreneurs, executives, lawyers, chefs and beauticians, the newspaper said.
Besides the unemployed, those on the lowest rungs of the income ladder were retired people and those working for struggling enterprises, it added.
"The market plays an important part in personal earnings," it said. "In addition, under a transitional economy, unfair competition and policy loopholes can allow some people to make fortunes."

Hundreds of millions of Chinese have boosted their incomes and living standards under sweeping economic reforms launched in the late 1970s. But some people have reaped the benefits of economic reform before others.
